entries.note: Used in the 14th century like [[methinks]], but meaning 'it seems to me'; Jess wants to bring it back to fill a lexical gap.
A Middle English word, used into the 19th century, meaning 'soon afterwards'; Jess suggests reviving it.
An old word for a year, one of several lost time frames that Rob thinks make perfect sense.
The Old English word for an hour before the French import [[hour]]; it matches similar Germanic words such as German Stunde.
In Britain a billion used to mean a million million; now it routinely means a thousand million, as in American usage.
A lost word for a thousand million, from the time when a British [[billion]] meant a million million; the hosts joke it sounds like mallard.
Means 10,000; Rob says both the noun use 'a myriad of' and the adjective use have been valid since the 16th–17th centuries, despite viewer criticism.
The Old English name for February, meaning 'mud month'.
The Old English name for March, which Jess says meant a quick month, or a month of nimbleness and activity.
The Old English name for April, 'Easter month'.
An Old English month name, probably May, so called because cows could supposedly be milked three times a day then.
The Old English name for November, 'blood month', when early Saxons sacrificed and butchered animals to store as food for winter.
An old word for Friday evening, the eve of Saturday.
A 13th-century word for dawn; Jess says it reminds her of the video game Skyrim.
A fairly transparent lost word meaning the day of one's death.
A 14th-century word for a clockmaker, from the same source as [[hour]].
An old word for a timepiece, sundial or hourglass; Rob compares it with the French word for a clock, and it is related to [[horologer]].
An old word for a butcher, used before English took [[butcher]] from French.
From French; originally someone who dealt only in goat meat, since a [[buck]] was a male goat, which also relates it to [[springbok]].
Despite sounding heroic, it meant someone who habitually made money from spurious lawsuits, something like an ambulance chaser.
An old nickname for a doctor, from the practice of judging someone's health by examining their urine, probably in the 16th–17th centuries.
An old word for a pimp.
An Old English term for a carpenter, before the French word [[carpenter]] took over; Rob thinks it makes more literal sense.
Formed many old job titles for makers, also used figuratively as in poemwright; Rob says it is related to [[wrought]].
An old word for a baker, one of many [[wright]] job titles.
An old word for a soldier, one of many [[wright]] job titles.
An old word for a builder, one of many [[wright]] job titles.
Rob's favourite [[wright]] title; the pudding would have been a savoury dish made with suet, though he likes to imagine trifle sponges.
A French word that originally meant someone who made carriages and carts, so [[treewright]] makes more literal sense; [[cartwright]] is an alternative.
An alternative word for a maker of carts, like the original meaning of [[carpenter]]; it now survives mostly as a surname.
An old word for a midwife, and also a nickname for a pickpocket.
A very old word: 'mid' means with and 'wife' originally meant woman, so it is the person who is with the woman.
Fairly modern US slang for someone who talks too much, quoted from the Philadelphia Saturday Evening Post in 1910.
A Latin-derived coinage from [[ventus]], 'wind', found from the 14th to 19th centuries, meaning either excess wind or figurative windbaggery; Washington Irving used it.
Originally a woman who spun thread for a living, using the feminine [[-ster]] ending; unwed women of certain ranks traditionally took up spinning.
An agent-noun ending, gender-neutral now in trickster and gangster, but specifically feminine in Middle English, unlike the neutral or masculine -er.
A woman who sewed for a living, before the French-derived -ess ending gave seamstress; formed with [[-ster]].
A woman who bleached cloth, formed with the feminine [[-ster]] ending.
Originally a woman weaver, now a surname; formed with the feminine [[-ster]] ending.
Originally a woman brewer, now a surname; a female brewer Rob interviewed insisted on the title, and there was a UK pub chain called Brewsters.
From bakester, a woman baker, with a spelling change that hides it in plain sight; now a common surname, including in Jess's family.
One of Rob's favourite old names for a spider, essentially 'web spinner' with a fancy verb form.
An old word for a spider, similar to the French [[araignée]] and from the same Latin root.
An old word for a spider meaning 'venom head', related to [[cobweb]] but not to adder; Jess notes it appears in The Hobbit.
Related to [[attercop]]; it simply means a spider web, since a spider could also be called a cop.
An old job title for a sword maker, since a bilbo is a type of sword; the hosts note the Hobbit connection.
An old word for a spider, like a little walking weaver, since [[gang]] was an old way of saying walk.
An old word for a rabbit, possibly behind the name [[Coney Island]].
Perhaps named for its rabbit ([[coney]]) population, or after another place that was named for its rabbits.
An old word for a [[porpoise]], used before English adopted the word porpoise.
Means 'pig fish', fitting its blunt rounded snout; the hosts revisit an error from a previous episode about whether dolphins are porpoises.
From French, originally Greek, meaning 'shadow tail' and possibly related to [[obscure]]; supposedly the longest one-syllable word in English.
The Old English word for a squirrel; the first part means oak, and the best guess for the whole is 'oak dweller', compare [[Eichhörnchen]].
German for squirrel, which Rob thinks involves folk etymology; like Dutch and other Germanic words for squirrel, it relates to the oak, as does [[acweorna]].
An old name for the [[giraffe]], a 'camel leopard'; it is also the name of a southern hemisphere constellation.
Comes from Arabic zarafa; Middle English also had other names like [[gerfaunt]] and [[orafle]].
A brief Middle English name for the [[giraffe]] whose ending was influenced by [[elephant]], a typical ending stuck onto exotic animals.
Another Middle English name for the [[giraffe]], probably from a Latin rendering of the same Arabic word.
An old word for either a rhinoceros or a unicorn, meaning anything with a single horn; Rob found it in Herbert Coleridge's dictionary.
An old synonym for openly from Herbert Coleridge's dictionary, related to [[aperture]].
An old word from Coleridge's dictionary meaning confused or perplexed; a relative survives as northern English dialect [[mither]].
A northern English dialect word meaning to bother someone, which Rob says is a relative of [[bemoidered]].
A prefix popular in the 15th–16th centuries, usually meaning around or on all sides (besiege, bespatter) but sometimes privative, as in behead.
Meant to thrash someone very soundly; one of the [[be-]] words Jess wants brought back.
Meant to thrash someone verbally; formed with the [[be-]] prefix.
To make a fool of someone; a [[be-]] word that still comes up a little today.
Meant to insult someone; it sounds like filling them with joy, but actually means making them the object of [[mirth]].
Doing something of your own accord without any real cause; it made Rob snort and blush.
An old verb meaning to displease someone.
An old term meaning pregnant; its etymology is uncertain, but Rob thinks it is probably related to [[blossom]].
An old word meaning to give birth to a child, to bring forth.
A crude word from Francis Grose's 1785 Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue for a man whose scrotum hangs longer than his penis.
A Grose word, supposedly related to [[rantallion]], for a sexual position with the woman on top facing the opposite direction.
Means having beautiful buttocks, named after the [[Callipygian Venus]], a statue whose reattached head looks back over her shoulder at her behind.
A Francis Grose word for a little white lie.
An old, fanciful word for a liar: someone who specializes in falsehoods.
An old word for a liar, implying someone who adds figurative wrinkles to the truth.
An old word for a liar, which Jess says kind of makes sense; she learned it from the card game League of the Lexicon.
One of several old words for a liar whose logic Jess doesn't fully understand yet.
Another old word for a liar that Jess lists, without explaining its logic.
Someone who stubbornly insists they're right; spread by Erasmus's story of a priest who kept saying 'mumpsimus' instead of 'sumpsimus' in 'quod ore sumpsimus'.
An old word for a scarecrow from Coleridge's dictionary, which reminds Rob of [[emmet]].
Used in southwest England as an insult for people not from the area, especially tourists.
A medieval word for a stranger, meaning someone who has come; one of the [[-ling]] words discussed in an earlier episode.
A fit of the blues, or sometimes a vague abdominal pain; its exact origin is unknown.
Describes someone who snores a lot, one of many old words for bodily conditions.
Belching; Rob recalls a dictionary, possibly Johnson's, describing it as a gassy, meaty-smelling emission.
A rare word meaning to spit on something, probably a fanciful Latinate formation related to [[sputum]]; quoted from the Saturday Review on the Shakespeare–Bacon craze.
From Latin iactare, 'to throw', meaning to swagger, boast or thrash in your sleep; it sounds naughtier than it is, like [[ejaculate]].
Now has an almost solely crude meaning, but originally just meant to exclaim.
An old imitative word for a fight or uproar, like [[bobbery]] and [[foofaraw]], from the same family as hullabaloo and kerfuffle.
An old imitative word describing the sounds and actions of fighting, like [[hubble-shubble]].
An old imitative word describing the sounds and actions of fighting, like [[hubble-shubble]].
A Middle English word meaning to dance gracelessly, without skill but perhaps with enjoyment; one of Jess's two words to bring back.
Means to hide oneself in a corner, what you might do if you don't feel like [[balter|baltering]]; Jess wants it back.
Rob thought it was obscure, but it is widely known in the US, with many spelling variants such as cattywampus.
